Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: 72 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Alex Moore (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (Orion ML Infra), Sara Liu (Orion CTO), Jamal Thompson (Orion SRE), Anita Rao (Orion Security)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): SE walked through kernel heuristics and runtime lanes. Customer asked about CUDA graph instability with persistent KV cache and heavy bursty traffic. Action items captured.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Okay, uh, thanks everyone for joining. We're gonna do a sort of runtime lane analysis, priya's gonna lead on the profiling side, and Diego will chime in for the bench harness. Michael, Sara, nice to meet you all.
[00:18] Michael: Hey thanks, yeah we gave a quick background in the deck, but to reiterate — we run a mix of short-chat requests plus long-context summarizations and that mix is what makes batching unpredictable.
[00:30] Priya: Right, and that mixture is where kernel selection ends up oscillating between the vLLM path and the TensorRT-LLM optimized kernels. We'll show traces where evictions and kernel swaps add 10-30 ms tail.
[00:45] Jamal: For us the main worry is sometimes the CUDA graph replay fails and you drop back to slower kernels causing a cascade. We've seen it especially when KV cache growth crosses a threshold.
[01:05] Priya: Yeah, that's a classic. There's a few heuristics — persistent KV cache sizing, when to prefetch, and the graph replay window. On RTX-class hardware you'll see one behavior, on A100/NVLink you'll see another. We instrumented both in our bench harness.
[01:28] Sara: Can you clarify the difference people keep saying — TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM in practice? We care mostly about latency SLOs under 95th and 99th percentiles.
[01:40] Diego: Short version: TensorRT-LLM gives more aggressive fused kernels and lower steady-state per-token cost for large batch lengths and static seq lengths, vLLM tends to be more flexible with dynamic batching and can have faster cold-starts because it avoids some heavy compile steps. But there are many caveats — CUDA graph usage, quantization readiness, and KV cache semantics.
[02:05] Michael: So for our workload with spiky bursts, which will win?
[02:12] Priya: It depends — if your requests are small and latency-critical, vLLM's eviction-aware scheduler with small-batch optimizations often edges out. But if you can pin sequence lengths and amortize compile overhead, TRT-LLM wins at scale. Also, TRT-LLM's fused attention is sensitive to sequence length variance.
[02:36] Anita: From the security side, we need to keep all traffic inside our VPC, and keys must use our KMS — any on-prem deployment must support HSM integration. SOC2 and audit logging are must-haves.
[02:54] Alex: Totally — Redwood Private supports customer KMS and HSM integrations. We'll share the VPC checklist and SOC2 artifacts after the call.
[03:06] Jamal: Back to the runtime — we noticed a phenomenon we called "kernel thrash" where the runtime keeps flipping kernels every few seconds during high diversity prompts. Could you explain how Redwood runtime avoids that?
[03:18] Priya: Sure. We have a lane predictor that classifies requests by token length distribution and recent sequence history. It tries to keep requests on a compatible kernel lane; if it detects a sustained mismatch we trigger a soft migration window rather than instant swap. But under very bursty traffic you can still see oscillation.
[03:37] Diego: And on top of that there's the CUDA graph replay — if the graph is invalidated due to dynamic shapes or KV cache chop, we fall back to a slower path and recompile. That window is where tail latency spikes.
[03:55] Michael: Is the graph replay deterministic? We saw intermittent failures where it would fall back and then compile again and then fail after 10 minutes.
[04:05] Priya: Not fully deterministic — it depends on kernel-level op ordering and memory alignment. Some drivers will be stricter. We add sanity checks and use a replay template to reduce churn, but there's still edge cases. We're tracking a small class of bugs that appear on particular driver versions with TensorRT.
[04:29] Sara: How does quantization affect this? We want to try 8-bit and maybe 4-bit for cost but worried about quality/regressions and perf anomalies.
[04:39] Priya: Quant can change kernel choices — certain fused kernels aren't available at 4-bit, so runtime falls back to different paths which can increase latency variance. Our optimize tool recommends quant profiles per model and per workload; we can run a quick A/B on your model.
[05:02] Jamal: If we go on-prem, network between nodes is over our private NVLink cluster, but we also have some RPC calls over the VPC. Any issues with KV cache consistency across nodes?
[05:16] Diego: KV cache sharding across NVLink is fine, but remote pulls can add jitter. We recommend a local hot-cache strategy: keep most-frequent prefixes pinned to local GPU memory and fallback remote fetch with async prefetch. That reduces tail.
[05:35] Michael: Could you show an example trace?
[05:39] Priya: Yeah, let me pull up a trace from the bench harness. (screen) Here — you can see a spike at T+38s where CUDA graph invalidated, runtime fell back, recompiled, and you get a 120 ms tail. Then when KV cache occupancy hits 75% we start evicting oldest prefixes and cold prompts get longer.
[06:02] Priya: Note the pattern — frequent small prompts interleaved with long-context completion cause repeated evictions, causing the kernel lane predictor to flip often.
[06:15] Michael: Hmm. Could a smarter prefetch prevent eviction chain? We have reuse patterns for a subset of customers.
[06:22] Priya: Yes — if you can provide hot-prefix lists we can pre-pin those to GPU memory and adjust eviction thresholds. Also batching policies matter: two small requests batched into one can reduce per-token cost but may violate latency SLOs if not streamed properly.
[06:41] Alex: On batching, one lever is continuous batching with latency caps — Redwood can cap how long a request waits to form a batch and prioritize SLOs. There's also adaptive batch size that considers current KV cache footprint.
[06:56] Jamal: Any specific kernel-level signals we should capture on our end to help debug?
[07:02] Priya: Collect per-request chosen kernel id, seq length, KV occupancy, CUDA graph version id, and driver/kernel errors. Also GPU mem high-water, and if possible cupti traces for a few samples. We'll give you a schema.
[07:18] Michael: We'll prod that — we can give you a sample of 48 hours of traces.
[07:23] Alex: Great. Quick question on cost: does TRT-LLM generally save more per-token cost after quant and fusion?
[07:31] Diego: In our experience with steady-state long sequences, yes — the fused kernels and int8/4 quantized paths reduce flops and memory bandwidth, so per-token unit cost is lower. But you pay with less flexibility and longer compile times.
[07:47] Sara: Regarding failure modes: do you have automatic fallback policies if a model path fails? We can't afford routing to a wildly different model that changes output dramatically.
[07:56] Priya: We do prioritized fallbacks — first we try model-compatible smaller variants (same tokenizer/optimizer), then a functional fallback that maintains schema. Also there are cost-aware fallbacks and controlled A/B for quality preservation.
[08:15] Anita: For security compliance, can you ensure audit logs include token metadata and redaction? We can't log raw PII.
[08:24] Alex: Yes, we support token-level redaction, audit logs, and retention policies. We'll send the compliance pack.
[08:32] Jamal: On NVLink tests — we want to reproduce your multi-GPU path where kernel routing uses NVLink to keep KV shards local. Can Redwood orchestrate that?
[08:44] Diego: Absolutely, we'll run an NVLink harness. We also want to test stress cases where you force KV churn to observe eviction behavior.
[08:55] Michael: What's the timeline for a pilot if we sign on? We want to do a 4-week pilot with some reserved capacity.
[09:03] Alex: Typical pilot is 2–4 weeks. We'll provide a bench harness, remote profiling, and a small reserved pool. Pricing and SOW follow.
[09:12] Sara: Any gotchas running on our on-prem? We run RHEL and a custom kernel and older NVIDIA drivers.
[09:19] Priya: Driver versions matter a lot. We'll send a compatibility matrix. Older drivers may make CUDA graph replay flaky and some TRT plugins won't work. We can ship a recommended container and a driver checklist.
[09:32] Michael: Can we keep some inference in our VPC and burst to Redwood hosted for overflow? Hybrid routing.
[09:39] Alex: Yes, hybrid routing is supported — you can set policy by region, tier, or cost. Redwood can route to hosted as a fallback for capacity spikes, with data handling rules you configure.
[09:52] Jamal: If hosted fallback is used, how do you guarantee data residency?
[09:57] Alex: We have region controls and can restrict fallbacks to specific regions. For strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[10:07] Michael: Let's talk concrete bench steps.
[10:11] Diego: We'll run three suites: 1) steady-state long-seq with TRT-LLM quantized, 2) mixed short/long burst with vLLM dynamic batching, 3) forced KV churn stress test across NVLink. We'll compare p50/p95/p99 and also kernel-swap counts and graph replay rates.
[10:32] Priya: We'll also instrument for sequence variance and report average graph invalidations per hour.
[10:39] Sara: Good. On the legal side, procurement will want to see terms and data processing addendum.
[10:46] Alex: I'll loop in our commercial team and send standard documents.
[10:51] Michael: Anything else on tuning?
[10:54] Priya: One more tip — for models that have a long KV prefix and then short queries, consider splitting the serving path: keep prefix on a warm GPU and route short requests to another lane with a lightweight cache. It reduces eviction thrash.
[11:11] Jamal: That split approach might work for our top 10 customers. We'll surface hot-prefix lists.
[11:18] Diego: Great. We'll need exact prompt samples to reproduce.
[11:22] Michael: We'll share.
[11:25] Alex: Okay, let's summarize next steps and owners.
[11:29] Priya: Action items on the notes. Bench harness, traces, NVLink test planning, security review.
[11:36] Sara: Thanks everyone. This was very helpful.
[11:40] Alex: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials and schedule the NVLink run.
[11:45] (call ends)
